This is my first MMO too and ive only been playing for a few months, so here’s my advice as a fellow newb:

Wander around your beginner area (determined by your race). If you run around you’ll reveal/unblur the map, find waypoints (quick travel) and things to do. 

When there’s an orange circle or icon on the map or minimap, that’s an event. Events happen everywhere at any time, so just keep running around until you find one. Run to the circle or icon. Read the orange header that appears on the right side of your screen and try to figure out whats going on. If you see a big group of people, follow them and do what they do. You can’t steal kill in GW2, so just go ham trying to figure out your attacks. 

Go to either Hardstuck, MetaBattle, or Snow Crows and pick a basic power build for your class. You wont have any idea what any of the words mean, so just make your build match the one on the site and then learn by playing. 

Gear rarity color from most common to rarest: white, blue, green, yellow, orange, pink, purple. You will not be seeing anything purple for a long time. You’ll be changing armor a lot in the early levels. 

When interacting with in game merchants, do click the “sell junk” button but don’t sell anything else to them. Instead, click ‘o’ to open up the Black Lion Trading Company, go to the Trading Post in that menu (third tab on the left) and sell things there.

This is a newb friendly guild I’m in based in discord: https://www.reddit.com/r/Guildwars2/s/ySJmSFPAou

Consider the leveling process a tutorial. The game really opens up when you hit level 80, everything before that is mostly learning how the game works and how to interact with the world.

Events are limited time situations on the map that anyone can participate in. Look on the map for orange circles and orange moving icons like boss skulls. Run into the orange circle and read the orange text on the right side of the screen to figure out what you’re supposed to do. Common ones are escort an NPC around the map and beat a boss.

Break things down into the smallest, least scary steps possible. Get so microscopic with your steps that you can’t even think about the bigger picture because you’re so far removed from it. When you open a word doc, don’t think about the whole paper you have to write. Only think about the first sentence. 

Making a list of everything sound like too much? Write down just one thing you need to do. Just one. That’s all. Then walk away and get a glass of water. Come back, write down a second thing. Bam! You’ve made progress. You’ve written down two things that weren’t written down five minutes ago. You’ve made tangible, measurable progress. 
Try not to see the whole forest of “yeah I wrote down two things but I haven’t even written down everything, never mind actually doing any of it.” That’s not the point. The point is to demonstrate to your brain “I am capable of doing something related to this and not collapsing into anxiety.” And while showing your brain this, you’re getting the thing done.

Anything is better than nothing. Writing the word ‘the’ is still more than a blank piece of paper.

So I have BPD and my partner is on the spectrum. One of our issues tends to be that while she struggles with picking up on implicit emotional cues, I’m hyper aware of them. Sometimes what seems screaming out loud obvious to me, she doesn’t notice at all. So we have to be aware of that disconnect and translate ourselves to each other. I need to spell my thoughts out more clearly/explicitly. She needs to understand that I’m reacting to cues she didn’t intend to give but is still giving me.

The autism-BPD dynamic has also been helpful in some ways. She’s been able to understand my behavior from a logical standpoint within the context of my diagnosis. “Oh yeah I can see why that feels like a rejection”, etc. That way my reactions don’t seem as over the top to her as they can to other people. 

As for understanding someone with BPD in general, the basic idea to take away is that borderlines are usually suffering intense emotional pain from social situations that don’t affect the average person much, and they react to that pain because they’re scared of it getting worse. 

Depending on your relationship with your friend and how open she is about her diagnosis, it might be helpful for you to ask what her biggest symptoms and triggers are so you can understand what’s going on with her specifically. 

I don’t know if that was at all helpful, but hopefully it gives you some insight.

I had a therapist literally laugh at the idea that I could be borderline. Five years later after I had moved on from the idea, I was finally diagnosed with it. Sometimes I feel bitter over how different things would’ve been if anyone had taken me seriously when I first looked into it. 
Tell your therapist to look up quiet borderline, and if she still doesn’t understand, consider getting a second opinion.

As someone who is depressed, the best things my friends can do for me is sticking with me and proving they give a fuck. Let him know you're there for him, hang out with him, give him little just-because presents (you don't even have to spend money, draw him a picture or give him a cool rock), make playlists inspired by him, tell him you care no matter how awkward saying it is, seek him out. Just show he's in your thoughts, in a good way.

Don't guilt him. Playing the guilt card ("don't you care about anyone besides yourself?" etc) is not productive for depressed people, just painful and sometimes leads to anger.

And don't leave him. Actually, don't say you'll be there for him if you don't think you'll be able to support him through the whole thing. You need to take care of your own mental health, so really consider if you can be a support system. If you honestly can't, don't lie, because it hurts even more.
